title: Cultural Dimensions of Fake News Exposure: A Cross-National Analysis Among European Union Countries
screen_reason: Secondary analysis of Flash Eurobarometer 464 (2018) across 25 EU countries (N = 24,551). The Results section reports the share of respondents saying they come across news or information that misrepresents reality or is false 'every day or almost every day' - 33.9% across the whole sample, with country figures for Spain (53%), France (39.5%) and Portugal (32.5%). That is self-reported RECALL of exposure with a threshold share and an explicit denominator, which §1 admits.

estimates.country: 25 European Union countries (the 28 EU members minus Cyprus, Malta and Croatia)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they come across news or information that misrepresents reality or is even false every day or almost every day
estimates.value_raw: The mean value for the whole sample (33.9%)
estimates.denominator: 24,551 respondents across 25 EU countries (Flash Eurobarometer 464, 2018; mean 982 per country, minimum 505 in Luxembourg, maximum 1,015 in Great Britain)
estimates.definition: Answered 'Every day or almost every day' to 'How often do you come across news or information that you believe misrepresent reality or is even false?' (4-point scale: every day or almost every day / at least once a week / several times a month / seldom or never)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'following an audience perspective, we will define fake news in this article as false or distorted information'
estimates.source_quote: The mean value for the whole sample (33.9%) indicates the high level of penetration of the fake news phenomenon in the perception of EU citizens broadly, but is also a sign of the great disparity between countries (see for a complete description, Online Supplementary Material, Graph S1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own perception of how often they encounter false or reality-distorting news; no external verification. The authors stress this is 'subjective perception, not objective exposure' and cite the known problems of self-report exposure measures (Prior, 2009). Standard Eurobarometer sampling and fieldwork (TNS Political & Social); response rate not reported in this paper
estimates.moderator_quote: To carry out the study, we use data from the Flash Eurobarometer 464 survey conducted by the TNS Political and Social Network in 2018 about fake news and disinformation online... Twenty-eight European Union (EU) countries were included in the sample, but we selected 25 for which the six Hofstede's dimensions scores are available, excluding Cyprus, Malta, and Croatia. The total sample was N = 24,551.
estimates.notes: POOLED row. Whether 33.9% is the share across all 24,551 respondents or the unweighted mean of the 25 country shares is not stated ('The mean value for the whole sample'); the wording suggests the latter, so an adjudicator should treat it as a 25-country average. The three country rows below are components of this same pooled figure - use EITHER the pooled row OR the country rows, not both, when aggregating. The paper also reports the item's scale mean (M = 2.18, SD = 1.12 on the reversed 4-point scale), which is a scale score, not a share, so no row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Vague country statements with no point value were NOT turned into rows: 'In EU countries like Spain, Greece, and Hungary, more than 50% of the population believes that they are exposed... every day or almost every day' and 'this occurs for less than 20% of citizens in countries like Sweden or Finland'. Greece, Hungary, Sweden and Finland therefore have only bounds (>50%, <20%), and the per-country figures live in Online Supplementary Material Graph S1, which is not in this text. (2) Digital News Report 2018 figures quoted in the introduction (Brazil 85%, Spain 69%, Germany 37%, Netherlands 30% concerned about what is real and fake online) were NOT extracted - they are cited from Newman et al. (2018), i.e. figures from elsewhere (R8), and measure concern, not encounter frequency. (3) The dependent variable's scale mean (M = 2.18, SD = 1.12) is a scale score with no share attached and so yields no row. (4) HLM coefficients (masculinity beta = .005; uncertainty avoidance beta = .004; social media use beta = .156, etc.), ICC values and R-squared are associations, not prevalence. (5) The survey also asked about self-rated ability to identify fake news and whether false information is a serious problem, but no shares for those items are reported in this text.

rob.design: Secondary multilevel analysis of an existing probability-based cross-national survey: Flash Eurobarometer 464 'Fake News and Disinformation Online' (TNS Political & Social, 2018). 25 of the 28 EU countries retained (Cyprus, Malta and Croatia dropped for lack of Hofstede scores); N = 24,551, mean 982 per country (min 505 Luxembourg, max 1,015 Great Britain); 'the study followed the standard practices of sampling and fieldwork of Eurobarometer surveys'. No response rate, weighting scheme or fieldwork dates are reported in this paper. Outcome is a single self-report item; the authors explicitly flag it as subjective perception rather than objective exposure and acknowledge the known problems of self-reported exposure (Prior, 2009). Only 25 level-2 units, at the lower limit for multilevel country effects (addressed with REML and Satterthwaite adjustment).
rob.item6_quote: In the survey, respondents in each country were asked, "How often do you come across news or information that you believe misrepresent reality or is even false?" The participants responded to this query on a four-point scale: 1 = Every day or almost every day, 2 = At least once a week, 3 = Several times a month, and 4 = Seldom or Never.
rob.item10_quote: In EU countries like Spain, Greece, and Hungary, more than 50% of the population believes that they are exposed to news or information that misrepresents reality or is even false every day or almost every day... The mean value for the whole sample (33.9%) indicates the high level of penetration of the fake news phenomenon in the perception of EU citizens broadly.
